headline: North Rip Turning Green and Cold — Albies Showing, Fluke Peaking, Bass Starting to Stack
subhead: The water off the Southwest Ledge dropped a few degrees this week and the whole island bit down at once — false albacore, September fluke, and the first real push of migrating bass.
body_markdown:
You feel it before you see it out here — a little more chop on the ebb, a little more bite in the wind swinging out of the northwest overnight, and the light changing color over the Southwest Ledge by six in the morning. That's the tell. The island runs on its own clock, and this week it told you fall is closing in fast. Water temps across the region have started sliding — Kings Point sitting at 70.9, New London down to 69.4, Montauk reading 69.1 — and while Block Island's own numbers run their own way surrounded by open ocean, that cooling trend from the Sound out to the Point is exactly the signal that gets everything moving out here: bait tightening up, structure loading with fish, and the whole system compressing around the rips.

Fluke has been the best story of the year right now, not a leftover from summer. The Ledge has been holding fish in that 30 to 50-foot range on the softer bottom just off the rock pile, and boats working slow drifts with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4 to 1-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, have been putting keepers in the box on the last two hours of the ebb when the current lays down enough to hold bottom contact. It's not a blitz, it's a working bite — you have to stay on the drift, keep the rod tip low, and feel for that extra weight rather than a hit. But it's been steady enough that the mates at the docks are calling it the best fluke stretch of the season, and there's no reason to think that ends before the water pushes into the low 60s.

The albie run is the other half of this week's story, and it's the one we flagged a week ago — said the fall push would build fast and that this stretch of water would be the first stop for anyone chasing them, and that's exactly what's happened. Fish have shown in real numbers off the North Rip and out along the Southwest Ledge, working bait pods in short, violent bursts and then going quiet for twenty minutes before showing again fifty yards away. Small metal is doing the work — half-ounce to 3/4-ounce epoxy jigs in that translucent green-and-white pattern, Deadly Dicks, and small Albie Snax on light spinning gear. The trick with these fish hasn't changed in thirty years: get ahead of the breaking fish, don't cast into the middle of them, and work the edges where the bait's getting pushed rather than the center of the commotion. Best window has been the last two hours of the incoming, right as the rip starts to build current against the tide change.

Striped bass are the slower-moving piece, but the staging pattern is real. We said last week that bunker schools were tightening up from Raritan Bay through Narragansett Bay under the building moon and that bass were starting to show genuine interest rather than picking at stragglers — and that's the pattern setting up around here too. Bigger fish are starting to shadow the bunker schools moving past the North Rip and staging off the deeper edges of the Ledge in 40 to 60 feet, not committing hard yet but clearly positioned. Bunker chunks fished on the bottom with a fish-finder rig have picked off a few better fish in the 20 to 30-pound class on the outgoing tide near the Ledge, and there's early tube-and-worm success trolled slow along the rock structure at first light. This is a pattern that should only get stronger as the moon builds this week and tidal range increases — more water movement means more bait pushed off the flats and into the rips, and that's when the bigger bass really start to commit.

Bluefish have been mixed — some real chopper-class fish mixed in with the albie blitzes on the Ledge, especially when metal gets worked a little faster and shallower than you'd fish it for the albies alone. Nothing like the bunker-driven blitz action building down around Montauk this week, where a near 18-and-a-half-pound blue took a tournament, but the size class moving through this area has ticked up, and it's worth keeping a heavier wire leader rigged if you're working the same water as the albies — you'll get bit by both.

Looking at the next few days: the moon's building toward the next phase, which should mean more tidal push through the rips by the weekend, and that's good news across the board — more current means more bait concentrated on structure, which means more committed bass and a better shot at sustained albie action rather than the on-again, off-again pattern of this week. If the wind stays out of the northwest and holds under 15 knots, the Southwest Ledge and North Rip should both fish well on the morning tides. If it swings east and builds, expect the albies to scatter and the fluke bite to hold better than the surface action. Either way, this is the stretch of the calendar Block Island waits all summer for — the water's cooling, the bait's getting nervous, and the fish know it.
